For example, when they say they'll give 20% off on something, they give this discount on the condition that the person accepts and buys it right there in the store. It's the same when landing projects. If you tell a client you can do something (at no extra cost) two weeks earlier than the norm, and you see they don't appreciate it and easily pass it by, take a look at your calendar and say, 'I made a mistake.' So they learn to appreciate it when they get a good concession. You might lose out in some places, but in the long run it has many benefits. This rule is followed at all levels of negotiation, from everyday transactions to equations and international relations, and it should be.

Written by: Sahand Iranmehr

Eurydice had died once. Orpheus was allowed to bring her back from the underworld; but right at the threshold of freedom, he looked back and lost her forever. Sometimes history's plan for those whose fate is tied to an inevitable death is exactly this: it gives a dead thing a chance to return—not to revive it, but so that its death becomes final this time.

Perhaps "57" was not an absolute end for the monarchy—or whatever other name was later given to it; it was a historical wound whose final fate could still be doubted. Then "57" will no longer be just the date of the monarchy's fall; it could become the moment when the idea of monarchy, after a second chance, lost the possibility of return forever.

Orpheus lost Eurydice once more because he looked back right at the brink of her revival. Perhaps some political dreams are like that too: they fail once, but they get a second chance not to return, but to die for good.

Sometimes an idea does not die from its first crushing defeat and blow, but from the way its followers choose to resurrect it.
